clue.text: Biblical structure with awfully wet floor circling infant

indicators.note: Awfully means badly, and letters set down badly do not stay in the order they were handed over in.
To circle a thing is to go right the way around it, so the shuffled letters close up on both sides of what comes next.

parts.note: the eight letters of wet floor in a new order, ready to open up near the end
a babe is an infant

explanation.surface: An old ruin whose soaking wet floor runs all the way round a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tower of Babel is the tower Genesis has humanity build towards heaven, the one that ends with everyone speaking different languages. 'Awfully' reads as an intensifier on 'wet' and is the instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tower of Babel is a building described in Genesis, so 'Biblical structure' names it by the book it comes from and the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Next number hard to hold

indicators.note: To hold something is to keep it inside you, so the letter named goes within the word doing the holding.

parts.note: ten is a number
H is the grade stamped on a hard pencil

explanation.surface: A figure coming up that is difficult to keep hold of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Next number' reads as one phrase and only the first word of it defines; the second is the figure that does the holding. H for hard is the pencil grade printed on the side.
explanation.definitionFit: Then means at the time following this one, so what happens then is what happens next.

clue.text: Amount of power in the time of steam?

parts.note: James Watt made the steam engine practical, and the unit of power was later named after him
an age is a stretch of time

explanation.surface: A question about how much power was to be had back when steam drove everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The steam age belongs to Watt, so 'the time of steam' is his age twice over — the era named after the engineer and the letters of his name plus AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Wattage is the number of watts a machine draws or delivers, which is an amount of power measured in the usual unit.

clue.text: Mountains the place for shooting practice?

definitions.note: 'Mountains' is plural where the answer is singular: a range is the whole line of them, so the plural picture and the single word name one thing.
definitions.meaning: peaks standing in a line along a skyline are spoken of by one collective word
the long strip of ground a rifle club sets aside for its targets

explanation.surface: Hill country that doubles as somewhere to practise your aim.
explanation.walkthrough: A shooting range and a mountain range are one word doing two jobs, and the clue sets them end to end with no join at all. The question mark flags that the second half describes the ground, not the practice.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a line of mountains, and a range is also the stretch of ground laid out for target practice, both everyday senses of the one word.

clue.text: Plump insect he's somehow trapped

indicators.note: Somehow means by some means or other, which leaves the letters free to arrive in any order at all.
Something trapped is shut in with no way out, so those letters finish up enclosed by the word around them.

parts.note: a fly is an insect
the three letters of he's in another order

explanation.surface: Somebody has managed to trap a fat insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plump' sits where an adjective describing the insect would sit, which is exactly where the clue wants to leave it; it is the definition standing on its own. The apostrophe in 'he's' counts for nothing once the letters move.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleshy means carrying plenty of flesh, the kinder-sounding word for plump.

clue.text: Expects fool to lead injured emus

indicators.note: To lead is to go in front, so the fool's letters take the head of the answer.
Something injured has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked about no longer sit where they did.

parts.note: an ass is a fool
the four letters of emus in another order

explanation.surface: A fool being put in charge of a flock of hurt emus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Injured emus' is the sort of picture that sticks in the head, and the birds are only four letters. 'Expects' opens the sentence as though somebody in the story is doing the expecting.
explanation.definitionFit: To assume something is to take it as read before it happens, which is what expecting it comes to.

clue.text: Acquires vases, it's said

indicators.note: 'It's said' points at the sound of a word rather than its spelling, so you hear the answer instead of reading it.

parts.note: urns are vases, for ashes or for flowers, and spoken aloud they are the answer

explanation.surface: A report that somebody is picking up vases.
explanation.walkthrough: Urns are the crossword's standard vase and turn up constantly at five letters or fewer. 'It's said' works twice over — gossip on the surface, instruction underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn something is to acquire it by working for it, a narrower way of saying the same thing.

clue.text: Left out cheese for the worms

indicators.note: Out of order is the sense wanted here: the word beside it has come out of the arrangement it was in.

parts.note: L is the standard short form for left
the six letters of cheese in another order

explanation.surface: Cheese forgotten on the side until it is fit for nothing but the worms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out' reads as one phrase about neglected food, and the two words belong to different jobs. Leeches are annelid worms, the ones doctors once used for bleeding patients.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeches are segmented worms of the annelid family, so the plural 'worms' covers them straight.

clue.text: Wheat entirely consumed in this

indicators.note: 'This' is the clue itself, so 'in this' says the letters are sitting in the words you are reading.

parts.note: the answer runs across the join, from the end of wheat into the start of entirely

explanation.surface: A whole crop of wheat finished off.
explanation.walkthrough: A hiding place is hardest to see when the cover words read naturally, and 'wheat entirely' is a phrase anybody might write. 'In this' points at the clue rather than at anything in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been eaten has been consumed, two past participles that swap freely at the table.

clue.text: Set reel in motion at film studios

definitions.note: Elstree is one place rather than several studios: the name stands for the studio complex there, which English always speaks of in the plural.

indicators.note: Letters set in motion will not stay where they were put, so the two words beside it can land anywhere.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Somebody starting the projector rolling at a film studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set reel in motion' is precisely what you would say about getting a projector going, which is why the letters lie so quietly in it. Elstree is the Hertfordshire studio town north of London where the Star Wars and Indiana Jones films were shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Elstree names the town whose studios have been turning out British films since the 1920s, so the place stands in for the studios themselves.

clue.text: Confront consequences of being a conductor?

parts.note: the everyday idiom: standing there and taking whatever is coming to you
read as the price of the job, and meant flatly — the conductor spends the whole concert looking at the music

explanation.surface: What the conductor of an orchestra has to answer for when the evening goes badly.
explanation.walkthrough: A conductor stands with the score in front of him and the players' parts all round, so the idiom is literally true of the job every night. The question mark is the setter owning up to the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: To face the music is to front up to the blame or punishment that is coming, which is confronting the consequences of what you did.

clue.text: A drug distributed in Paris

indicators.note: To distribute is to spread things out into new places, which is what has happened to these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A drug being handed out around the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' reads as where the handing out happens rather than as the seven letters to work with. The definition is the two words at the front, article and all.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirin is the household painkiller, so 'a drug' names it by its class, from the most familiar member of it.

clue.text: Mountain expert's turn of phrase

indicators.note: A turn is a change of direction, and letters given a turn come round in an order of their own.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A mountaineering expert with a distinctive way of putting things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn of phrase' is such a settled expression that its middle word vanishes into it, which is where the instruction hides. Sherpas are the Himalayan people whose men have guided and carried on Everest since the first expeditions.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sherpa is a member of that Himalayan people, so 'mountain expert' defines them by the work they are famous for rather than by ancestry.

clue.text: Does it make some of the creeper go laterally?

definitions.text: Does it make some of the creeper go laterally?

indicators.note: 'Some of' asks for a part instead of the whole, and the part wanted is a run of letters lying inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the answer runs from inside creeper, through go, into the start of laterally

explanation.surface: A gardener wondering whether the climbing plant will be trained sideways.
explanation.walkthrough: A pergola is the frame of posts and crossbeams a climbing plant is trained along, so the sentence describes the answer and hides it in the same words. There is no separate definition to hunt for.
explanation.definitionFit: A pergola carries a creeper out along its horizontal beams instead of letting it climb, so the whole question describes what one does.

clue.text: States capable of being useful

parts.note: the States is the United States, US for short
able means capable

explanation.surface: Countries that can be counted on to pull their weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capable of being' is the wording a dictionary uses to define the answer, so the sentence reads as one plain definition and gives nothing away. The States is the usual British way of saying the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Something usable can be put to use, which is what calling a thing useful claims for it.

clue.text: Wound round cross, after gold compound

indicators.note: Round says one piece is laid the whole way about another, closing on both sides of it.

parts.note: a bite is a wound

indicators.note: After puts the cross behind the gold, so those two letters stand in that order before anything wraps them.

parts.note: Au is gold's symbol on the periodic table
a cross is written X, as on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: Something wound round a cross and set behind a lump of gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' is the past tense of wind on the surface and a noun — an injury — underneath, and that switch is what the clue is built on. Bauxite is the reddish ore aluminium is smelted from.
explanation.definitionFit: Bauxite is a mass of hydrated aluminium oxides, so 'compound' names the ore by its chemistry rather than by the mine it comes out of.

clue.text: In China, use aspirin for queasiness

indicators.note: In says the letters are already inside the words that follow, needing nothing done to them.

parts.note: the answer runs from the end of China through use to the first letter of aspirin

explanation.surface: Taking aspirin while in China to settle a turning stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: Aspirin has already been an answer at 11 down, which makes the word look like a leftover rather than a hiding place. A comma never interrupts a hidden answer; the letters run straight through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nausea is the sick feeling in the stomach that queasiness names.

clue.text: Secluded room of private Tuscan building by motorway

indicators.note: To build is to put pieces together into something new, so the letters are re-laid instead of left as they came.

parts.note: an inner thought is a private one
the six letters of Tuscan with M for motorway added, re-laid as one word

explanation.surface: A private villa in Tuscany that happens to stand beside a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuscan building' paints a whole villa in two words, and neither word is doing what it looks like. M is the motorway letter British drivers see every day on the M1 and the M25.
explanation.definitionFit: An inner sanctum is the private room at the heart of a place, which only the favoured few get into, so 'secluded room' says what it is.

clue.text: Naturist holds note as a gentle reminder

indicators.note: To hold something is to keep it inside, so the note sits within the word that does the holding.

parts.note: a naturist goes nude
the musical notes run A to G, and any of those letters can be clued as a note

explanation.surface: A naturist clutching a note by way of a polite hint to somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is one of the smallest words in the crossword and nearly always a letter from A to G. A nudge really is the gentlest reminder there is — an elbow rather than a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudge is a small push in the ribs meant to remind you of something without anyone having to say it aloud.

clue.text: Sacred oath conceals something to believe in

indicators.note: To conceal is to keep out of sight, so the answer lies covered by the words on either side of it.

parts.note: the answer runs from inside sacred into the first letter of oath

explanation.surface: A solemn oath with a belief buried somewhere inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacred oath' is already a phrase about belief, so the words feel like part of the definition rather than the cover. Credo is Latin for 'I believe', and an English credo is the statement of what somebody holds to.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is the set of beliefs a person or a church lives by, so it is exactly something to believe in.

clue.text: Why people will display excessive publicity

indicators.note: To display a thing is to put it where it can be seen, and these words have the answer showing right across them.

parts.note: the answer runs from the second letter of why into the start of people

explanation.surface: The reason people go in for shameless self-promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence promises to explain why people behave like this and never does, which is the sign to stop reading it as a sentence. Hype is the trade's word for the noisy overselling of a film or a record.
explanation.definitionFit: Hype is publicity laid on far thicker than the thing deserves, which is the excess the definition points at.

clue.text: Popular entrances under cover

parts.note: the in thing is the popular one
doors are entrances

explanation.surface: Well-liked doorways sheltered from the weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular entrances' reads as one phrase about doorways people like, and its two words belong to separate pieces. Under cover here means inside, out of the rain, rather than in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: To be indoors is to be inside a building, which is what being under cover means when the weather is the worry.

clue.text: Regularly appearing on tendril, fly will enlighten

indicators.note: Letters that appear regularly come at a fixed interval, and the interval a setter means by it is every second one.

parts.note: take the second letter and every other one after it: tEnDrIl FlY

explanation.surface: An insect that keeps landing on the same curl of a climbing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma between tendril and fly belongs to the surface alone; the count runs straight through it and on into the next word. 'Regularly' always means every other letter, and here the counting starts on the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To edify someone is to improve their mind or their morals, which is enlightening them.

clue.text: Upset? Eat beer can to give dietary aid!

indicators.note: Something upset has been tipped over, and what was in it comes out in no particular order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: Somebody feeling ill being told to chew a beer can and feel better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset?' opens like a question put to the reader, the way an advertisement for indigestion tablets does, and it is the instruction. Beta-carotene is the orange pigment in carrots that the body turns into vitamin A.
explanation.definitionFit: Beta-carotene is sold in tablets as the source the body makes vitamin A from, so 'dietary aid' names it by what people take it for.
